newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Cash-strapped Zimbabwe launches tax blitz.
newsitem.headline: Cash-strapped Zimbabwe launches tax blitz.

text.p: Zimbabwe's cash-strapped government on Tuesday announced measures to improve tax collection and net evaders and defaulters who it said cost millions in lost revenues.
Finance Minister Herbert Murerwa said the steps, effective immediately, included door-to-door registration of businesses and companies to bring defaulters and delinquents to book.

"The department (of taxes) intends to address the issue of defaulting and delinquent taxpayers and bring these into the net. It intends to intensify registration of taxpayers using door-to-door methods," he told a news conference.

"As the aim of the exercise is to spread the tax burden and help reduce the budget deficit, members of the public are all urged to cooperate with the department in order to make the exercise a success," he said.
Zimbabwe's budget deficit has remained stubbornly above a target of five percent annually under Western-backed economic reforms the government embarked on in 1991.
Local economists blame runaway government spending, which accounts for about 40 percent of gross domestic product, for keeping the deficit high.

Murerwa reiterated that the government was unlikely to cut the deficit to 8.5 percent of GDP it was aiming for in the 1996/97 financial year ending on June 30, from 10.1 percent in 1995/96, because of pay awards last year to civil servants.
On tax collection, he said: "The current situation is unacceptable because we have many companies registered but only a small proportion are paying taxes."

Murerwa and Tax Commissioner Gershem Pasi decline to say how much the government was losing through tax evasion, but Pasi said out of a total of 77,000 registered companies, only 33,000 were on the department's tax books.
Murerwa said the tax department would intensify pay as you earn (PAYE) audits to speed remittance of tax and increase audits to curb under-declaration or non-declaration of benefits and payments.
